claims.text: The base material is a Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi high-entropy alloy.
The Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi alloy typically crystallizes when as-cast under rapid cooling.
A variant containing approximately 2 atomic percent oxygen can be formulated as (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2.
The added oxygen occupies interstitial sites in the alloy.
The alloy can be processed by drop-casting into a water-cooled copper mold.
Drop-casting into a water-cooled copper mold suppresses equilibrium crystallization in this alloy.
Oxygen addition produces short-range ordered oxygen complexes within the alloy matrix.
Short-range ordered oxygen complexes hinder long-range atomic rearrangements.
Localized oxygen complexes act as pinning centers.
Oxygen-induced pinning increases the kinetic barrier to crystallization.
The increased kinetic barrier broadens the supercooled liquid region.
Adding approximately 2 atomic percent oxygen enhances the glass-forming ability of Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi.
The oxygen-doped alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate for amorphous-phase formation than the undoped alloy.
The oxygen-doped alloy will exhibit a wider supercooled liquid region than the undoped alloy.
The beneficial effect of oxygen exists only over a narrow oxygen-concentration window.
Oxygen contents above the optimum may promote oxide phase separation or excessive ordering that counteracts glass formation.
A lower crystallization-onset temperature is an indicator of oxygen-enhanced glass-forming ability.
Prior data do not directly establish the oxygen-concentration range or magnitude of glass-forming improvement in TaNbHfZrTi.

contradictions.description: The mechanism claims that oxygen raises the kinetic barrier to crystallization and reduces crystallization tendency, but the falsification rule treats a lower crystallization-onset temperature as evidence of improvement. A lower onset temperature generally denotes earlier crystallization and is directionally inconsistent with the stated stabilization mechanism unless separately justified.
